issue_context.title: Incorrect handling of ClientHello messages without signature_algorithms extension (e.g. TLS 1.1 or TLS 1.0)
issue_context.body:
When negotiating TLS 1.2, it's permissible to send a ClientHello that omits the `signature_algorithms` extension.
Specifically, when the extension is omitted, the server is supposed to behave as if support of SHA-1 signatures was advertised, see [section 7.4.1.4.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5246#page-47).

Problem exists when the OpenSSL server is configured not to support SHA-1 signatures. In such case, when a ClientHello without the `signature_algorithms` extension is received, the server aborts the connection with `illegal_parameter` Alert. At the same time, when an equivalent ClientHello, with `signature_algorithms` extension listing just SHA-1 mechanisms is received, it's rejected with the expected alert: `handshake_failure`. Also, when the server is reconfigured with support for SHA-1 signatures, an extension-less ClientHello is accepted.

Note that this happens for connections that use RSA key exchange, where server does not perform any signatures...

Using current master (pre-beta1): bfd6b619b6ccba

Reproducer:
```
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa -keyout /tmp/localhost.key -out /tmp/localhost.crt -subj /CN=localhost -nodes -batch
openssl s_server -key /tmp/localhost.key -cert /tmp/localhost.crt -www -sigalgs RSA+SHA256:RSA+SHA384:RSA+SHA512:ECDSA+SHA256:rsa_pss_pss_sha256:rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 -no_renegotiation -cipher DEFAULT:@SECLEVEL=0
```
In another console:
```
git clone https://github.com/tomato42/tlsfuzzer
pushd tlsfuzzer
git clone https://github.com/tlsfuzzer/tlslite-ng .tlslite-ng
ln -s .tlslite-ng/tlslite tlslite
git clone https://github.com/tlsfuzzer/python-ecdsa .python-ecdsa
ln -s .python-ecdsa/src/ecdsa ecdsa
PYTHONPATH=. python3 scripts/test-sig-algs-renegotiation-resumption.py --no-renego
```
tlsfuzzer output:
```
...
without signature_algorithms and signature_algorithms_cert ext ...
Error encountered while processing node ExpectServerHello() (child: <tlsfuzzer.expect.ExpectCertificate object at 0x7f38245e4af0>) with last message being: <tlslite.messages.Message object at 0x7f3824571430>
Error while processing

    runner.run()
  File "/home/hkario/dev/tlsfuzzer/tlsfuzzer/runner.py", line 232, in run
    raise AssertionError("Unexpected message from peer: " +
AssertionError: Unexpected message from peer: Alert(fatal, illegal_parameter)

...
```
OpenSSL output:
```

read R BLOCK
read R BLOCK
```

When the SHA-1 is disabled and DH ciphersuites are the only advertised by client, the server handles it even worse, by sending `internal_error` Alert message.

Reproducer (server side is the same):
```
PYTHONPATH=. python3 -u scripts/test-sig-algs-renegotiation-resumption.py --no-renego -d
```

tlsufzzer output:

This also happens when the OpenSSL server and client are configured to make a TLS 1.0 connection but SECLEVEL doesn't permit SHA-1 signatures, the server then sends `internal_error` Alert.

review_comments: This one really is an internal error -- it's the case where the peer didn't send siglalgs, so we try to use the defaults.  We had an error retrieving the defaults, so we failed internally before we could try any form of negotiation.
isn't the default SHA-1, and if SECLEVEL is set sufficiently high, it will fail?

Yes.
Clients that want to work in a modern (web) environment need to not rely on the server using the defaults.
I'm not seeing an argument that this point in the code is anything other than an internal error, though.

my point is that this happens when a legitimate client (that supports just RSA ciphersuites, doesn't advertise supported sig_algs, advertises TLS 1.2 as the highest supported version) connects to a legitimate server (that has support for SHA-1 disabled)

now, either in such situation we shouldn't get internal_error, or this code shouldn't get executed in the first place

do you mean the latter?
Well, speaking formally, "insufficient_security" if we have fetched the defaults but rejected them because of SECLEVEL will fit better. But I tend not to distinguish it here.

That's no longer a legitimate client in this day and age.
Effective participation in the modern TLS ecosystem requires sending supported sig_algs.
However, this is not the code that will cause the handshake failure in that scenario; that would be a few lines later when we actually check against the default values.  This is just doing a database lookup for what the default value should be, and that lookup "should" never fail.

@kaduk If you look at tls1_get_legacy_sigalg(), you can see that there is a call to tls12_sigalg_allowed() which in turn calls the security level check. So this is definitely not just a database lookup and this change is IMHO correct.

Okay, thanks for nudging me to look more closely at `tls1_get_legacy_sigalg()`, I do see the security-level checks at the end of the function.  That said, there are still plenty of codepaths that can return NULL for reasons other than the security check, so it seems to me that there are codepaths where either alert is more correct, and thus neither the current code nor the current state of the PR is truly "correct".

Factoring out the `tls12_sigalg_allowed()` call into `tls_choose_sigalg()` itself is not a trivial fix, since then it would duplicate work with `tls12_shared_sigalgs()`.  Pushing the SSLfatal() calls up into `tls1_get_legacy_sigalg()` would be more mechanical but doesn't seem terribly pretty either.
IMO giving handshake failure in some cases where an unlikely internal error event happened is harmless. So I am OK with the PR as is.
This one seems like a good change; we are doing a negotiation, just using the protocol default for the peer's offer, and found no overlap.  That's a handshake failure, not an illegal parameter.
